I will keep my land centered on the winter wheat and summer maize rotation. In Quzhou County, that is still the most reliable way for me to balance yield, water use, labor efficiency, and market security. The local pattern is very clear: most farmland is already in this rotation, rainfall is concentrated in summer, and irrigation pressure is heavier in the wheat season. Because of that, I will not spread myself across many small crops. I would rather run one system well. I will use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed, keep fertilizer rates moderate but not loose, irrigate wheat several times and maize only when the season turns dry, return residues, and rely on rotary tillage for wheat establishment and no-tillage for maize after wheat harvest. I will also keep pesticide use restrained and based on field pressure, because I care about cost control and soil condition as much as output. My target is stable high grain production, not experimentation for its own sake.

This is also consistent with the local production direction in Quzhou County, where winter wheat-summer maize remains the dominant system and recent county-level work has focused on higher-efficiency wheat-maize management with water and fertilizer integration. Sources: China Agricultural University Quzhou Experimental Station on the county’s promoted wheat-maize technology and local wheat conditions ([1](https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/2/25/art_46232_1012984.html), [2](https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/2/22/art_46317_1012731.html)); Quzhou site description and climate characteristics in published research ([3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5290742/)).
